candidates.quote: The words of truth are naturally simple, and justice needs no subtle interpretations, for it has a fitness in itself; but the words of injustice, being sick in themselves, require clever treatment.
candidates.author: Euripides
candidates.locator: line 469, opening of Polyneices’ speech, in The Complete Greek Drama, vol. 2 (Random House, 1938)
candidates.speaker: Polyneices
candidates.whyThisMonth: It is the month’s thesis spoken on a stage: what is true can be said plainly, and only a crooked case needs clever handling.

candidates.quote: It is this, let me tell you—that the strongest man in the world is he who stands most alone.
candidates.author: Henrik Ibsen
candidates.locator: Act V, Dr. Stockmann’s last speech, the closing words of the play
candidates.speaker: Dr. Stockmann
candidates.whyThisMonth: The play is about a man who tells his town what is in its water, and this is the sentence he ends on: worth having before a day when you may be the only one saying it.

candidates.quote: The truth is rarely pure and never simple.
candidates.author: Oscar Wilde
candidates.locator: First Act, his answer to Jack’s ‘the whole truth pure and simple’
candidates.speaker: Algernon Moncrieff
candidates.whyThisMonth: A joke that is also a warning against the tidy version of events, and it takes four seconds to read.

candidates.quote: My way of joking is to tell the truth. It’s the funniest joke in the world.
candidates.author: Bernard Shaw
candidates.locator: Act II, his reply to Nora Reilly
candidates.speaker: Peter Keegan
candidates.whyThisMonth: Keegan answers a compliment by naming his method, and the method is the whole month.

candidates.quote: We live close together and we live far apart.
candidates.author: Susan Glaspell
candidates.locator: the one act, Mrs Hale’s speech near the close, in Plays (1920)
candidates.speaker: Mrs Hale
candidates.whyThisMonth: Two women in a cold kitchen see what the men cannot, and this is the line where one of them admits how little she had looked.

candidates.quote: Do any human beings ever realize life while they live it?
candidates.author: Thornton Wilder
candidates.locator: Act III, her question to the Stage Manager
candidates.speaker: Emily Webb
candidates.whyThisMonth: Emily asks the one question that turns an ordinary morning into a thing the reader is actually awake for.

candidates.quote: O wad some Power the giftie gie us / To see oursels as ithers see us!
candidates.author: Robert Burns
candidates.work: To a Louse, On Seeing One on a Lady’s Bonnet at Church
candidates.locator: final stanza, lines 1 to 2, Poems, Chiefly in the Scottish Dialect (1786)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The oldest prayer in the language for clear sight, and it is aimed at the reader rather than at anybody else.

candidates.quote: I’m nobody! Who are you? / Are you nobody, too?
candidates.author: Emily Dickinson
candidates.locator: lines 1 to 2, Poems by Emily Dickinson, Second Series, ed. Todd and Higginson (Roberts Brothers, 1891), Life I
candidates.whyThisMonth: A cheerful refusal to perform: at six in the morning it lets the reader be exactly as small as they are.

candidates.quote: Earth’s crammed with heaven, / And every common bush afire with God: / But only he who sees, takes off his shoes; / The rest sit round it, and pluck blackberries, / And daub their natural faces unaware / More and more, from the first similitude.
candidates.author: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
candidates.locator: Seventh Book, the ‘Earth’s crammed with heaven’ passage
candidates.speaker: Aurora
candidates.whyThisMonth: The month’s central claim in verse: the world is already full, and the whole difference is whether you look.

candidates.quote: I, too, dislike it: there are things that are important beyond all this fiddle.
candidates.author: Marianne Moore
candidates.whyThisMonth: A poet opens her most famous poem by admitting she dislikes her own art, which is what honesty sounds like before flattery gets to it.

candidates.quote: The universe is made of stories, / not of atoms.
candidates.author: Muriel Rukeyser
candidates.locator: section IX, The Speed of Darkness (Random House, 1968)
candidates.whyThisMonth: Two lines that tell the reader what they are actually made of, which is a steadying thing to hear early.

candidates.quote: The door itself / makes no promises. / It is only a door.
candidates.author: Adrienne Rich
candidates.locator: closing three lines, Snapshots of a Daughter-in-Law: Poems 1954 to 1962 (W. W. Norton, 1963)
candidates.whyThisMonth: Plain speech about a choice that is genuinely open: nothing is promised, and the door is still a door.

candidates.quote: Although the wind / blows terribly here, / the moonlight also leaks / between the roof planks / of this ruined house.
candidates.author: Izumi Shikibu
candidates.locator: the poem beginning ‘Although the wind’, in The Ink Dark Moon: Love Poems by Ono no Komachi and Izumi Shikibu (Scribner, 1988)
candidates.whyThisMonth: A thousand years old and completely exact: the same gap that lets the cold in is the one the light comes through.

candidates.quote: Why can’t I tell the true shape of Lu-shan? / Because I myself am in the mountain.
candidates.author: Su Shi
candidates.work: Written on the Wall at West Forest Temple
candidates.locator: closing two lines, Selected Poems of Su Tung-p’o, p. 108 (Copper Canyon Press, 1994)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The clearest statement anywhere of why we misjudge the thing we are standing inside.

candidates.quote: My apologies to great questions for small answers.
candidates.author: Wisława Szymborska
candidates.locator: in Poems New and Collected 1957 to 1997 (Harcourt, 1998)
candidates.whyThisMonth: A poet apologising for the size of her answers, which is the right posture for anyone who wants to be believed.

candidates.quote: Myself when young did eagerly frequent / Doctor and Saint, and heard great Argument / About it and about: but evermore / Came out by the same Door as in I went.
candidates.author: Omar Khayyám
candidates.whyThisMonth: An honest report on years of argument that changed nothing: a useful check on a morning that wants to be clever.
